name: Dagster
summary: A data orchestrator that models persistent data assets and their dependencies in code, then coordinates runs through schedules, sensors, executors, and run storage.

features.name: Software-defined asset graph
features.description: Dagster asset definitions describe persistent objects and how to produce or update them; unlike bare ops, asset definitions carry dependency information.
benefits: Makes data products and their dependencies first-class orchestration objects
Keeps the intended data boundary close to the producing code
costs: The asset graph can obscure dependencies that occur outside the declared definitions
Materialization still depends on storage and IO-manager behavior

features.name: Event and time automation
features.description: Dagster provides schedules for time-based runs and sensors for event-based triggers, with the daemon responsible for evaluating these automation mechanisms in an OSS deployment.
benefits: Supports both periodic execution and data/event-driven execution
Separates trigger evaluation from the code that performs asset work
costs: Automation depends on daemon availability and correctly configured run coordination
Event-triggered systems require idempotence and cursor or deduplication policy

features.name: Durable run and event state
features.description: Dagster OSS deployments compose orchestration components with storages, executors, and a daemon; run and event records provide persistent coordination state for operations and observation.
benefits: Supports inspection and coordination beyond the lifetime of one worker process
Allows execution policy and storage policy to be configured at deployment boundaries
costs: The deployment has more components and operational state to manage
Stored run and event data require retention, migration, and access-control choices

mathematical_views.question: How can persistent data assets and their producing functions be ordered and selected for materialization?
assumptions: Declared asset dependencies form a graph with a usable execution order
Each materialization updates the asset boundary described by its definition
Storage side effects and external systems are represented by explicit resources or treated as graph boundaries

mathematical_views.question: How do schedules, sensors, and run records turn external observations or clock ticks into orchestrated runs?
assumptions: The daemon evaluates automation definitions and records enough state to avoid unintended duplicate work
A run has observable lifecycle states managed by the instance
The model abstracts executor-specific concurrency and failure-retry details

costs: Declared graph boundaries must be maintained as data systems evolve
Daemon availability and trigger idempotence become production concerns

benefits: Operational visibility and coordination across process lifetimes
costs: Persistent orchestration state increases deployment and retention complexity
